title: Unveiling Semiclassical Structures in Quantum Chaotic Eigenstates Using Neural Networks
authors: J. Montes, F. Borondo, Gabriel G. Carlo
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks and neural quantum states have consolidated a new paradigm to analyze and discover physical phenomena through constrained neural parametrizations. In this context, we investigate whether the semiclassical structure of the eigenfunctions of a quantum chaotic system can be unveiled through unsupervised learning. To this end, we train a "quantum dictionary", formulated as an overcomplete autoencoder, that sparsely represents the eigenstates of the system, using as an illustration the quantum baker map. The only explicit physical information imposed on the dictionary atoms is their localization in phase space, without providing any kind of information about the periodic orbits of the corresponding classical system. The model achieves high fidelity in reconstructing eigenstates not used during training. By comparing the learned atoms with an independently constructed "semiclassical dictionary", we find that they spontaneously localize on the periodic orbits and develop scar-like structures. This result is interesting in two ways: a localization constraint is sufficient to recover nontrivial semiclassical organization from spectral data and at the same time periodic orbits confirm their fundamental role in the structure of quantum chaotic eigenfunctions. More generally, our proposed architecture opens a new route to learning representations whose atoms optimize other chosen physical properties.
summary: The paper uses neural networks to learn an overcomplete dictionary representation for highly complex, chaotic quantum eigenstates. By constraining this learning process with phase-space localization, the model forces its learned building blocks (atoms) to spontaneously organize around structures corresponding to classical periodic orbits. This shows that simple geometric constraints can unlock deep semiclassical physics from purely spectral data.
main_problem: The study investigates whether unsupervised learning can reveal the underlying semiclassical structure of quantum chaotic eigenstates.
main_result: By imposing phase-space localization constraints on a neural network dictionary, the learned atoms spontaneously localize onto periodic orbits and develop scar-like structures, confirming their fundamental role in chaos.
method: The authors train an overcomplete autoencoder ('quantum dictionary') to sparsely represent eigenstates, comparing its learned structure against independently constructed semiclassical dictionaries based on periodic orbits.
model_or_system: The analysis uses the quantum baker map as a model for a quantum chaotic system. States are analyzed using phase-space representations like the Husimi density.
key_observables: Reconstruction fidelity ($F$), Hilbert-space overlap ($\Omega_{mr}$), and Effective Participation Number ($N_{	ext{eff}}$).
important_parameters: The dictionary size ($M$) relative to the state dimension ($D$), and regularization weights ($\lambda_G, \lambda_{loc}$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that phase-space localization constraints are sufficient to recover nontrivial semiclassical organization from spectral data.
figures_summary: Figures compare learned atoms' Husimi densities against known scar functions, showing structural alignment and high overlap ($	ext{SH} \approx 0.9$).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of characterizing chaotic eigenstates, details the autoencoder setup with localization constraints, presents the semiclassical dictionary construction, and concludes by comparing the learned structures to show emergent periodic orbit organization.
why_interesting: This work demonstrates a powerful data-driven method for extracting fundamental physical symmetries (like those dictated by classical periodic orbits) from raw quantum spectral data without explicit knowledge of the underlying Hamiltonian dynamics or symmetry operators.

The sparse dictionary network has widths D →M →D, with M > D. The active support is selected by residual correlations, as in complex orthogonal matching pursuit, and the decoder reconstructs the state by a least-squares recombination of the selected atoms. Training combines phase-insensitive reconstruction, dictionary-overlap diversity, and phase-space-localization losses.
